definition: Rational psychology is a historical philosophical term for the philosophy of spirit, or the philosophical study of human beings. In this older scheme, it stands alongside the philosophy of nature and theology as one of the main branches of fundamental philosophy.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Nature (philosophy of); pinned source text

reasons: The packet supports rational psychology as a co-ordinate branch of fundamental philosophy with theology and philosophy of nature, but it does not explicitly support the added generalization that these are 'the main branches.'

The packet supports only that “rational psychology or philosophy of spirit” is “co-ordinate with theology …” in connection with “Nature (philosophy of).” It does not support the definition’s framing of rational psychology as “a historical philosophical term” for the philosophy of spirit.

The packet says philosophy of nature is a branch of fundamental philosophy and that it is co-ordinate with theology and with rational psychology; it does not explicitly support the definition’s claim that rational psychology “stands alongside … as one of the main branches of fundamental philosophy.”

The packet does support the characterization “philosophy of spirit … (as philosophy of man),” but the definition adds additional claims about “philosophical study of human beings” and an “older scheme” that are not clearly stated in the supplied text beyond that brief parenthetical.
